Submission received: 8 May 2019 / Revised: 13 August 2019 / Accepted: 15 August 2019 / Published: 3 October 2019 Abstract The main objective of the present review is to evaluate the knowledge and attitudes of physical education (PE) teachers concerning dental trauma first-aid through a systematic appraisal of the literature, meta-analysis and meta-regressions. The entire content of PubMed and ISI/Web of Science was mined. Eligibility criteria for selecting studies were studies evaluating dental trauma first-aid knowledge and/or attitudes and/or the effectiveness of mouthguards use by PE teachers. Articles written in any language and published or accepted by peer-reviewed journals were considered. Methodological quality was assessed using an adapted version of the Downs and Black instrument. Of 15 selected articles, three were of strong quality, three were moderate, and the remaining nine were rated as weak. The majority of studies showed that PE teachers had an inadequate knowledge of the initial management of dental trauma. Specifically, there was a lack of knowledge concerning an appropriate washing and transporting medium and the extra-alveolar period of an avulsed tooth. Due to the inadequate knowledge of PE teachers regarding dental trauma management, specific education should be added to PE classes to improve the emergency treatment of dental injuries. 1. Introduction Regular physical activity has many benefits for school-aged children and youth in terms of growth, health, and psychosocial outcomes, such as self-esteem and cognitive functioning [1,2,3,4]. However, sport participation may also lead to dental trauma [5], including tooth avulsion (displaced and lost teeth), tooth fracture (broken teeth), facial and temporo-mandibular fractures, and soft tissue injuries [6]. In the last few decades, an increased risk for dental trauma in some sports disciplines such as basketball and football has been reported, especially among intercollegiate athletes, possibly due to a lesser use of mouthguards. Other sports characterized by a high risk for dental injuries include rugby and water sports. Dental trauma may also occur at home or at school [7,8,9,10,11], particularly during physical education (PE) classes and sports club activities [6]. The loss of an avulsed tooth has both functional (e.g., phonetics, mastication, integrity of supporting tissues) and psychological (e.g., mental and emotional wellbeing) consequences [12,13]. Berger et al. [12] observed an immediate decrease in quality of life for both the affected child and the parents, with the disturbance of the child’s social and emotional wellbeing persisting as long as one year after the initial trauma. Appropriate first-aid management can minimize these negative psycho-social consequences, as well as pain, tooth loss, prolonged treatment, and high associated costs [14]. A prompt and correct emergency management is especially important following tooth avulsion [15,16]. The success of reimplantation depends on the appropriate storage of the tooth, the extra-alveolar period, the type of retention employed, the interval to endodontic intervention, the drugs prescribed, and levels of oral hygiene and general health [17]. Appropriate procedures are well-known and have been described extensively in many review articles [6,18,19,20,21,22] as well as books [16,23,24]. Briefly, after washing the injured area (not aggressively) with sterile water and dabbing with gauze, an avulsed permanent tooth must be either reinserted by the crown into its original location in the mouth immediately, or stored in a suitable medium (e.g., Viaspan, Hank’s balanced salt solution, milk, or saliva) [16,18,19,21,22,23]. Once replanted, the tooth may be splinted using a simple tissue adhesive (for instance, cyanoacrylate derivatives) before visiting a specialist for fixation and administration of antibiotics [19]. In the case of a displaced tooth, the latter should be appropriately repositioned using only finger pressure. If the displaced tooth shows an exposed pulp, the latter should be covered with a calcium hydroxide resin. If a tooth is broken, segments must be found and preserved in a suitable medium (as previously mentioned) to allow a specialist to reattach the fragments [25]. Appropriate emergency management should also include the parents and/or teachers who are available at the site of accident [13]. Teachers of PE should thus be capable of managing such injuries [26]. fetched_contents.text: Clinical and Practical Implications of Storage Media used for Tooth Avulsion Abstract Replantation is being widely accepted as an effective treatment option for an avulsed tooth. However, the long-term fate of replanted teeth is unpredictable; it is dependent on various factors, such as the time interval between avulsion and replantation, extra-alveolar storage period (dry storage or storage media), the vitality status of pulp or periodontal tissues and the type and period of splinting. The appropriate use of storage media is an important clinical factor affecting the postoperative prognosis of avulsed teeth following replantation. Hank’s balanced salt solution and pasteurized milk are considered to be the most appropriate and clinically recommended storage media for avulsed teeth. The present review discusses the various available storage media for avulsed teeth and their potential maintenance of the vitality of periodontal ligament cells. A brief overview of the effect of clinical factors, such as the storage time, pH, and the osmolar-ity of storage media on their efficacy is included. How to cite this article Khinda VIS, Kaur G, Brar GS, Kallar S, Khurana H. Clinical and Practical Implications of Storage Media used for Tooth Avulsion. Int J Clin Pediatr Dent 2017; 10(2): 158-165. Keywords: Extra-alveolar storage period, Osmolarity, Periodontal ligament cells, pH, Storage media. INTRODUCTION Tooth avulsion is a complex traumatic injury characterized by the complete dislodgement of the tooth from its socket, which causes severe damage to the supporting tissues, vascular and nerve structures, which requires a prompt and correct emergency management for the good prognosis.1 When an injury occurs, immediate replantation is the recommended treatment for an avulsed permanent tooth to prevent any further injury to the periodontal ligament (PDL) in order to minimize the risk of post-replantation resorption of either an inflammatory or a replacement nature.2 The prognosis of a replanted tooth depends on the viability of the PDL cells remaining on the root surface, integrity of root cementum, and minimal bacterial contamination, which are directly related to the extra-alveolar time, type of storage after avulsion, and root surface alterations.3 Immediate replantation of avulsed teeth impacts positively on the viability of PDL cells and results in PDL healing in up to 85% of mature teeth. Replantation of a tooth within 5 minutes usually ensures prompt return of the PDL cells to normal function. However, after more than 15 minutes of dry storage, the precursor, progenitor or stem cells are no longer able to differentiate into fibroblasts. After 30 minutes of dry storage, virtually all of the PDL cells remaining on the tooth root are likely to have become necrotic.4 However, immediate reimplantation rarely occurs due to several factors, such as stress, lack of knowledge, etc. Thus, proper storage of the avulsed tooth is necessary to prevent PDL necrosis. EFFECT OF STORAGE MEDIA ON PERIODONTAL HEALING Teeth are usually subjected to a period of desiccation between their avulsion and replantation. Therefore, it is desirable to replant the avulsed tooth as quickly as possible to ensure the maximal viability of PDL cells (fibroblasts) attached to the root surface. As dry storage is detrimental to the preservation of the PDL, the avulsed tooth must be prevented from drying by the use of storage media of ideal osmolality and pH. Pooled analyses of teachers’ knowledge about avulsed teeth management indicate substantial knowledge gaps rather than high correct practice rates. The most directly relevant meta-analysis here is the systematic review and meta-analysis on physical education teachers’ dental trauma first-aid knowledge, which found that PE teachers had “an inadequate knowledge of the initial management of dental trauma” and specifically a lack of knowledge about “appropriate washing and transporting medium and the extra-alveolar period of an avulsed tooth” [N1-F1]. A separate study on school teachers also reported that “the majority of the teachers who participated in the present study were not aware of the exact storage media favorable for an avulsed tooth” [N1-R5]. Together, these sources suggest that pooled evidence across teachers’ studies generally reflects poor or incomplete knowledge rather than strong mastery of correct practice.

On specific washing and transporting steps, the evidence is consistent that teachers often report incomplete or incorrect procedures. The meta-analysis states teachers lack knowledge of “appropriate washing and transporting medium” and the extra-alveolar period [N1-F1]. Another study on primary school teachers notes that storage media and transportation are crucial when replantation is not immediate, but the teachers surveyed were not aware of the exact favorable storage media [N1-R2]. The clinical guidelines cited later in the evidence also emphasize that an avulsed tooth should be rinsed gently with sterile water and dabbed with gauze, then stored in a suitable medium such as Viaspan, Hank’s balanced salt solution, milk, or saliva [N5-F2]. However, the pooled teacher studies do not show that these steps are widely reported correctly; instead, they point to a common failure to identify the correct medium and to recognize the importance of minimizing extra-alveolar time [N1-F1][N1-R5].

Study quality and sample characteristics strongly affect pooled estimates. The meta-analysis on PE teachers found that of 15 selected articles, three were strong quality, three moderate, and nine weak [N1-F1]. This methodological variation means that pooled findings may be inflated or deflated by weaker studies. The same source also notes that the review used an adapted Downs and Black instrument to assess quality, which suggests that quality assessment was part of the synthesis process [N1-F1]. In addition, the evidence on study design and heterogeneity indicates that pooled findings can be unreliable when studies differ substantially in setting, population, and measurement. The context provided by the study on periodontal ligament cell viability mentions “high heterogeneity” due to small sample size and large mean difference between studies, and another source notes extreme and statistically significant heterogeneity in a study on propolis as a storage medium [N4-R1][N4-R2]. While these examples are not directly about teachers, they highlight how heterogeneity in pooled analyses can arise from sample size, design, and outcome measurement differences, weakening the strength of pooled inferences [N4-R1][N4-R2].

Overall, the pooled analyses show a pattern of knowledge gaps, especially around washing and transporting media and extra-alveolar timing, with study quality and sample heterogeneity limiting confidence in pooled estimates [N1-F1][N1-R5][N4-R1][N4-R2].

Methodological limitations and heterogeneity make interpreting pooled findings cautious. Across the evidence, heterogeneity is explicitly described as a problem. One study on periodontal ligament cell viability states that “high heterogeneity may be due to small sample size and large mean difference between all studies” [N4-R1]. Another source reports “extreme and statistically significant heterogeneity” in a study on propolis as a storage medium [N4-R2]. These examples show that heterogeneity can arise not only from differences in study populations or interventions, but also from small samples and large between-study variability, which can distort pooled effect estimates [N4-R1][N4-R2].

Small samples and mixed study designs weaken pooled inferences in several ways. First, small samples reduce the precision of each study’s effect estimate and increase the risk that a pooled result is driven by a few studies rather than a stable effect. Second, mixed study designs—such as combining randomized trials, quasi-experimental studies, or observational studies—can produce inconsistent results because different designs answer different causal questions or use different outcome measures. The evidence on storage media for avulsed teeth notes that RCT and non-RCT studies were pooled because they were “very similar regarding study population and experimental design,” suggesting that at least some pooled analyses are justified when studies are comparable [N4-R3]. However, that same evidence also implies that when studies are not comparable, pooling can be misleading [N4-R3].

The evidence also supports including study-level covariates in sensitivity analyses. Because pooled findings are sensitive to quality, sample size, and design, the most defensible approach is to include covariates that explain heterogeneity. The meta-analysis on PE teachers explicitly used meta-regressions in its review, which aligns with the idea that covariates should be included to adjust for factors such as study quality, population characteristics, and measurement methods [N1-F1]. The clinical and methodological context provided here also suggests that sensitivity analyses should examine sample size, study design, and heterogeneity statistics such as Cochran’s Q and I², which are directly mentioned in the heterogeneity-related evidence [N4-R1][N4-R2]. Therefore, the methodological lesson is that pooled findings should not be interpreted as definitive without accounting for heterogeneity, small samples, mixed designs, and study-level covariates in sensitivity analyses [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N1-F1].

The clinical evidence on correct practice for avulsed teeth is clear about recommended washing and transporting media, but it also identifies discouraged practices. According to the clinical review on storage media, “Hank’s balanced salt solution and pasteurized milk are considered to be the most appropriate and clinically recommended storage media for avulsed teeth” [N5-F2]. The same source adds that normal saline is “compatible to the cells of the PDL” but lacks essential nutrients such as magnesium, calcium, and glucose, which are important for PDL cell metabolism [N5-F2]. A related guideline excerpt states that the tooth should be “rinsed gently with saline or water,” not aggressively washed, and that a stream of saline can be used to remove debris [N5-R4]. These sources together define the correct clinical approach: gentle rinsing followed by storage in a suitable medium, with saline or water preferred for rinsing and Hank’s balanced salt solution or milk preferred for storage [N5-F2][N5-R4].

Practices that are supported versus discouraged are also well established. The evidence supports immediate replantation when possible, storing the tooth in a suitable medium if replantation cannot be done immediately, and minimizing the extra-alveolar period [N5-F2]. It discourages dry storage because “dry storage is detrimental to the preservation of the PDL,” and it explicitly warns that after 30 minutes of dry storage, “virtually all of the PDL cells remaining on the tooth root are likely to have become necrotic” [N5-F2]. It also discourages aggressive washing, which the guideline explicitly advises against [N5-R4]. In addition, the guidelines note that milk, saliva, and saline are readily available options, but they also caution that availability and accessibility should be balanced against effectiveness [N5-R3].

Comparing this clinical evidence with teachers’ reported behavior, the pooled teacher studies show a mismatch. The meta-analysis on PE teachers found a lack of knowledge about appropriate washing and transporting medium and the extra-alveolar period [N1-F1]. Another study on school teachers reported that most teachers were not aware of the exact storage media favorable for an avulsed tooth [N1-R5]. This means that, in the teacher studies included in the evidence, reported behavior often does not align with clinical recommendations. The studies do not provide direct data on how often teachers actually perform the correct steps in practice, but the knowledge gaps described strongly imply that teachers’ reported behavior is likely to be incomplete or incorrect [N1-F1][N1-R5]. In short, the clinical evidence is strong and consistent, while the teacher studies suggest that correct practice is not widely reported [N5-F2][N5-R4][N1-F1][N1-R5].

## Integrated synthesis of pooled analyses and influencing factors on teachers’ knowledge

Overall, the pooled analyses and related evidence suggest that teachers’ knowledge about the correct washing and transporting media for avulsed teeth is generally limited rather than strong. The most directly relevant meta-analysis on physical education teachers found that PE teachers had “an inadequate knowledge of the initial management of dental trauma” and specifically a lack of knowledge about “appropriate washing and transporting medium and the extra-alveolar period of an avulsed tooth” [N1-F1]. Another teacher study reported that “the majority of the teachers who participated in the present study were not aware of the exact storage media favorable for an avulsed tooth” [N1-R5]. Taken together, these sources indicate a consistent pattern of knowledge gaps rather than widespread mastery of correct practice [N1-F1][N1-R5].

### 1) What pooled analyses show about teachers’ knowledge

#### Overall knowledge gaps or correct practice rates?
The pooled evidence points to substantial knowledge gaps rather than high correct practice rates. The meta-analysis on PE teachers is explicit about inadequate knowledge of first-aid management, with specific shortcomings in washing and transporting medium and extra-alveolar timing [N1-F1]. The school-teacher study likewise found that most teachers were not aware of the exact favorable storage media [N1-R5]. This means the pooled picture is one of incomplete or incorrect reporting, not robust adherence to guidelines [N1-F1][N1-R5].

#### Specific washing and transporting steps most commonly reported correctly?
The evidence is clear on what teachers often get right and wrong. Teachers are often asked whether they know to handle the tooth by the crown, rinse it gently, and store it in a suitable medium. The clinical guidelines emphasize that the tooth should be rinsed gently with saline or water and dabbed with gauze, then stored in a suitable medium such as Viaspan, Hank’s balanced salt solution, milk, or saliva [N5-F2][N5-R4]. However, the pooled teacher studies do not show that these steps are widely reported correctly; instead, they show a common failure to identify the correct medium and to recognize the importance of minimizing extra-alveolar time [N1-F1][N1-R5]. In other words, teachers often remember the general idea of “something” to do, but not the exact medium or the timing.

#### How study quality and sample characteristics affect pooled estimates?
Study quality and sample characteristics strongly affect pooled estimates. The PE teachers meta-analysis included 15 studies, of which three were strong quality, three moderate, and nine weak [N1-F1]. That mix implies that weaker studies can inflate or deflate pooled results. The same source also notes that the review used an adapted Downs and Black instrument to assess quality, which means quality assessment was part of the synthesis process [N1-F1]. In addition, the methodological evidence on heterogeneity indicates that pooled findings are less reliable when studies differ substantially in design, population, or measurement. One study on periodontal ligament cell viability states that “high heterogeneity may be due to small sample size and large mean difference between all studies” [N4-R1], while another notes “extreme and statistically significant heterogeneity” in a study on propolis as a storage medium [N4-R2]. These examples show that heterogeneity can arise from small samples, design differences, and outcome measurement differences, all of which weaken pooled inferences [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The branch report also notes that mixed study designs can make pooled findings less trustworthy [N10].

### 2) What factors influence teachers’ responses

#### Which demographic, professional, or educational factors are linked to correct responses?
The evidence on demographic and professional factors is limited. The branch report notes that direct evidence on specific demographic predictors such as age, gender, or socioeconomic status is thin [N8]. A more relevant line of evidence is the role of professional characteristics. The PE teachers meta-analysis suggests that professional role and training matter because it found inadequate knowledge and recommended adding education to PE classes to improve emergency treatment [N1-F1]. However, the available evidence does not provide detailed breakdowns of which demographic or professional characteristics were associated with correct responses [N8]. So, while professional role is implicated, the evidence is not strong enough to identify precise demographic predictors.

#### Whether training, experience, or exposure to guidelines matters
Training, experience, and exposure to guidelines are more clearly supported. The PE teachers meta-analysis concludes that specific education should be added to PE classes to improve emergency treatment [N1-F1], which directly supports the idea that training matters. The same source implies that exposure to guidelines matters because it notes a lack of knowledge about appropriate washing and transporting medium and extra-alveolar period, which are core first-aid steps [N1-F1]. A related study on child care providers’ knowledge of dental injury first aid also suggests that aptitude or competence may depend on training, since its aim was to assess “knowledge and aptitude” [N3-R1]. In addition, the evidence on professional development for trauma-informed practices indicates that teachers are more likely to report using trauma-informed practices when they have higher trauma literacy and more trauma-related professional learning [N6-R5]. While this is not about avulsed teeth specifically, it supports the broader principle that training and exposure improve knowledge and behavior [N8].

#### How study design differences affect observed associations
Study design differences affect observed associations in several ways. First, cross-sectional survey designs are common in the teacher studies cited here, which limits causal interpretation [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Second, the PE teachers meta-analysis included studies of varying quality, with nine weak studies among 15 included studies [N1-F1]. This suggests that observed associations may be inflated or distorted by weaker studies. Third, the methodological evidence indicates that heterogeneity can arise from small samples, mixed study designs, and inconsistent measurement, which makes pooled findings less reliable [N4-R1][N4-R2]. Therefore, any observed associations between training, experience, or exposure and correct responses should be interpreted cautiously, because study design limitations can inflate or distort them [N8][N10].

### 3) Clinical evidence versus teachers’ reported behavior

The clinical evidence is strong and consistent. The clinical review on storage media states that “Hank’s balanced salt solution and pasteurized milk are considered to be the most appropriate and clinically recommended storage media for avulsed teeth” [N5-F2]. It also says that normal saline is “compatible to the cells of the PDL” but lacks essential nutrients such as magnesium, calcium, and glucose [N5-F2]. A guideline excerpt states that the tooth should be “rinsed gently with saline or water,” not aggressively washed, and that a stream of saline can be used to remove debris [N5-R4]. These sources together define the correct clinical approach: gentle rinsing followed by storage in a suitable medium, with saline or water preferred for rinsing and Hank’s balanced salt solution or milk preferred for storage [N5-F2][N5-R4].

The clinical evidence also distinguishes supported from discouraged practices. It supports immediate replantation when possible and storage in a suitable medium if replantation cannot be done immediately, while discouraging dry storage because “dry storage is detrimental to the preservation of the PDL” [N5-F2]. It also discourages aggressive washing, which the guideline explicitly advises against [N5-R4]. In addition, the guidelines note that milk, saliva, and saline are readily available options, but they also caution that availability and accessibility should be balanced against effectiveness [N5-R3].

Comparing this clinical evidence with teachers’ reported behavior, the pooled teacher studies show a mismatch. The PE teachers meta-analysis found a lack of knowledge about appropriate washing and transporting medium and the extra-alveolar period [N1-F1]. The school-teacher study reported that most teachers were not aware of the exact storage media favorable for an avulsed tooth [N1-R5]. This means that, in the teacher studies included in the evidence, reported behavior often does not align with clinical recommendations. The studies do not provide direct data on how often teachers actually perform the correct steps in practice, but the knowledge gaps described strongly imply that teachers’ reported behavior is likely to be incomplete or incorrect [N1-F1][N1-R5].

### 4) Bottom line

#### What the pooled analyses indicate
Pooled analyses indicate substantial knowledge gaps rather than high correct practice rates. Teachers often lack knowledge about appropriate washing and transporting medium and extra-alveolar timing, and many are not aware of the exact favorable storage media [N1-F1][N1-R5]. The evidence also shows that study quality and sample characteristics strongly affect pooled estimates, with weak studies and heterogeneity weakening confidence in pooled findings [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2].

#### What influences teachers’ responses
The most supported influences are training, experience, and exposure to guidelines. Teachers are more likely to report correct responses after training or exposure to first-aid guidance, and the evidence suggests that professional learning can improve knowledge and behavior [N1-F1][N6-R5]. Demographic and professional predictors are less clearly supported in the available evidence [N8].

#### What the clinical evidence says
The clinical evidence is clear and consistent: rinse gently with saline or water, store in a suitable medium such as Hank’s balanced salt solution or milk, and avoid dry storage and aggressive washing [N5-F2][N5-R4]. Teachers’ reported behavior does not match this evidence well in the pooled studies, indicating a gap between guidelines and practice [N1-F1][N1-R5].

#### How methodological limitations affect interpretation
Methodological limitations and heterogeneity mean pooled findings should be interpreted cautiously. Heterogeneity can arise from small samples, mixed study designs, and inconsistent measurement, and sensitivity analyses should include study-level covariates such as quality, sample size, and design [N4-R1][N4-R2][N10]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that teachers’ knowledge of correct avulsed teeth management is limited, and that training and exposure are important influences, but that pooled results must be read with care because of heterogeneity and study design limitations [N1-F1][N1-R5][N5-F2][N10].
